paragraphs: Bone and joint infection is easiest to manage when the anatomy, microbiology, source-control plan, and treatment intent are named explicitly. Acute, subacute, and chronic describe tempo. They do not, by themselves, determine antibiotic duration.
slides.notes:

Define what remains infected before choosing the treatment duration Bone and joint infection is easiest to manage when the anatomy, microbiology, source-control plan, and treatment intent are named explicitly. Acute, subacute, and chronic describe tempo. They do not, by themselves, determine antibiotic duration. Scope for the live session Teach through the core sections and three cases, then stop. The advanced section is a post-lecture reference for fellows, attendings, and questions that arise on service. Learning objectives Obtain useful cultures and identify urgent source control. Separate native-joint infection, PJI, osteomyelitis, and chronic wound colonization. Choose route and duration from the operative plan, retained material, and treatment intent. slides.title: Five questions organize every bone and joint infection
slides.section: Five questions organize every bone and joint infection
paragraphs: What is infected? Native joint, prosthesis, bone, spine, diabetic foot, pressure injury, or fracture hardware.
What is the best specimen? Blood, synovial fluid, bone, or multiple deep operative samples. A superficial wound swab rarely defines bone therapy.
What remains? Pus, necrotic bone, biofilm-coated implant, abscess, sinus tract, ischemic tissue, or an open wound.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Five questions organize every bone and joint infection What is infected? Native joint, prosthesis, bone, spine, diabetic foot, pressure injury, or fracture hardware. What is the best specimen? Blood, synovial fluid, bone, or multiple deep operative samples. A superficial wound swab rarely defines bone therapy. What remains? Pus, necrotic bone, biofilm-coated implant, abscess, sinus tract, ischemic tissue, or an open wound. Can it be controlled? Drain, debride, exchange, remove, reconstruct, revascularize, or manage noncuratively. What is the intent? Cure, treatment with retained material, chronic suppression, or treatment of acute flares only. Stable and unstable patients follow different clocks If the patient is stable, obtain the highest-value specimen before antibiotics. If septic, hemodynamically unstable, or neurologically threatened, obtain blood cultures promptly but do not delay active therapy or urgent source control.

slides.title: Diagnose
slides.section: A hot native joint requires aspiration, drainage, and active antibiotics
paragraphs: Aspirate promptly if feasible. Send bacterial culture, cell count with differential, and crystals. Obtain blood cultures when febrile, systemically ill, or bacteremia is plausible. Crystals do not exclude infection, and no single synovial WBC cutoff proves or excludes it.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
A hot native joint requires aspiration, drainage, and active antibiotics Diagnose Aspirate promptly if feasible. Send bacterial culture, cell count with differential, and crystals. Obtain blood cultures when febrile, systemically ill, or bacteremia is plausible. Crystals do not exclude infection, and no single synovial WBC cutoff proves or excludes it. Treat now After sampling, vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is a common empiric regimen. Substitute an antipseudomonal beta-lactam when resistant gram-negative risk is meaningful. Narrow once cultures return. Control the source Large-joint infection usually requires urgent orthopedic drainage. Failure to improve should prompt reassessment of drainage, adjacent osteomyelitis, and the diagnosis before automatic broadening or extension. Let the syndrome modify the empiric start Clinical setting Common pathogens Practical implication Typical adult native-joint infection S. aureus and streptococci Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is a common initial regimen after cultures. Older, immunocompromised, or suspected urinary/intra-abdominal source Enteric gram-negative bacilli in addition to staphylococci and streptococci Ensure gram-negative coverage and investigate the bloodstream source. Injection drug use, healthcare exposure, or penetrating/water exposure S. aureus ; consider Pseudomonas according to exposure and local epidemiology Use an antipseudomonal beta-lactam only when the risk is credible. Migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, or pustules Neisseria gonorrhoeae Obtain NAAT from exposed mucosal sites and culture purulent material; treat with ceftriaxone. Duration Uncomplicated, adequately drained large-joint infection is generally treated for several weeks, often about 3–4 weeks. Extend or redefine the course for bacteremia complications, adjacent osteomyelitis, delayed drainage, or poor response. Selected patients can transition to an active oral drug once improving. Sources sanjo , 2v4 , gono

slides.title: Establish the diagnosis
slides.section: In PJI, the operation determines what antibiotics can accomplish
paragraphs: A sinus tract communicating with the prosthesis is diagnostic. If stable, aspirate before antibiotics when results will change management. At surgery, obtain multiple deep tissue cultures. Do not build months of therapy around a superficial wound or sinus swab.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
In PJI, the operation determines what antibiotics can accomplish Establish the diagnosis A sinus tract communicating with the prosthesis is diagnostic. If stable, aspirate before antibiotics when results will change management. At surgery, obtain multiple deep tissue cultures. Do not build months of therapy around a superficial wound or sinus swab. Look for bacteremia Obtain blood cultures with fever, systemic illness, acute hematogenous presentation, or suspected S. aureus . Search for the bloodstream source and complications when bacteremia is present. PJI treatment pathways and antibiotic timing Strategy Best fit Published guidance and decision points DAIR with modular-component exchange Acute symptoms, fixed implant, no sinus tract, acceptable soft tissue, and a usable biofilm-active oral regimen. For staphylococcal PJI, the 2013 IDSA guideline describes an initial pathogen-directed phase with rifampin, then rifampin plus an active oral companion to complete 3 months for a hip or 6 months for a knee . Other organisms and situations require separate duration decisions. The IV-to-oral switch is individualized. One-stage exchange Selected chronic PJI with good soft tissue, known and tractable organism, and an experienced team. Duration depends on organism and regimen. IDSA describes 4–6 weeks of pathogen-directed therapy for nonstaphylococcal PJI and 2–6 weeks of IV therapy with rifampin followed by an oral companion and rifampin to complete 3 months for susceptible staphylococci. An active oral option may allow transition after initial treatment; no universal IV lead-in is established. Two-stage exchange: after explant and spacer Chronic PJI, compromised tissue, difficult organism, or failed retention strategy. IDSA recommends 4–6 weeks of pathogen-directed IV or highly bioavailable oral therapy after resection. Reimplantation timing depends on the clinical and operative assessment. Evidence does not establish a mandatory antibiotic-free interval. Reimplantation Proceed when the clinical, surgical, and microbiologic assessment supports control. Concordant positive deep cultures support persistent infection; a single virulent isolate can also be significant. Decide whether further therapeutic antibiotics are needed from the full operative and microbiologic assessment. With no residual infection, prolonged treatment is not automatic; indicated perioperative prophylaxis still applies. No curative surgery Operation is not feasible or is inconsistent with the patient's goals. Treat acute sepsis or bacteremia first. Then consider chronic suppression only when there is a defined pathogen, a tolerable active oral drug, and a meaningful goal. It is noncurative. Use “suppression” precisely The defined oral phase of a curative-intent regimen after DAIR is distinct from indefinite suppressive antimicrobial therapy. The 3-month hip and 6-month knee durations in the IDSA guideline apply to its staphylococcal rifampin-based regimen, not to every organism or regimen. Indefinite suppression is a separate, noncurative decision. Do not define DAIR candidacy by postoperative timing alone Symptom duration, implant stability, sinus tract, soft tissue, pathogen, host factors, and ability to exchange modular components all affect the chance of cure. Sources pji-2013 , pji-review , datipo

slides.title: Acute, subacute, and chronic osteomyelitis differ mainly in diagnostic and source-control problems
slides.section: Acute, subacute, and chronic osteomyelitis differ mainly in diagnostic and source-control problems
rows: Hematogenous infection, contiguous spread, or acute postoperative infection.
Blood cultures when relevant, drain abscesses, obtain deep cultures, and start active therapy promptly when ill.
Indolent vertebral infection or Brodie-type lesion; infection may mimic tumor or inflammatory disease.
If stable, obtain tissue for culture and histology before empiric therapy.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Acute, subacute, and chronic osteomyelitis differ mainly in diagnostic and source-control problems Use tempo to frame the problem, not to prescribe a duration Pattern Typical problem Immediate priority Acute Hematogenous infection, contiguous spread, or acute postoperative infection. Blood cultures when relevant, drain abscesses, obtain deep cultures, and start active therapy promptly when ill. Subacute Indolent vertebral infection or Brodie-type lesion; infection may mimic tumor or inflammatory disease. If stable, obtain tissue for culture and histology before empiric therapy. Chronic Sequestrum, sinus tract, devitalized bone, ischemia, or retained hardware. Define whether necrotic bone or hardware can be removed and whether soft-tissue coverage and perfusion can be restored. Route and anatomy predict the likely microbiology Syndrome Common pathogens Sampling implication Acute hematogenous long-bone or vertebral infection S. aureus most common; streptococci and enteric gram-negative bacilli according to host and source Blood cultures can be diagnostic. Evaluate S. aureus bacteremia for an endovascular source. Post-traumatic, postoperative, or hardware-associated infection S. aureus , coagulase-negative staphylococci, gram-negative bacilli; sometimes polymicrobial Use multiple deep operative specimens, not a surface swab. Contiguous diabetic foot osteomyelitis Mild/new: S. aureus and beta-hemolytic streptococci. Chronic, deep, or previously treated: gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes become more likely. Bone culture is preferred when feasible; superficial wound flora can mislead. Pelvic osteomyelitis beneath a pressure injury Often polymicrobial, but exposed bone and wound cultures are heavily colonized Deep bone obtained during planned debridement/closure is the useful specimen. Source Prefer blood cultures when hematogenous disease is plausible and bone or deep operative specimens when available. A superficial swab usually reflects colonizing flora. Duration With adequate source control and no retained implant, treatment generally does not exceed 6 weeks. Complete resection of infected bone may require no osteomyelitis course. Residual soft-tissue infection is treated separately. Route Osteomyelitis does not automatically require a PICC. An active, well-absorbed oral regimen is reasonable when the patient is stable, source control is adequate, absorption is reliable, and adherence and interactions have been addressed. Common anchors: most bacterial vertebral osteomyelitis, 6 weeks; diabetic foot osteomyelitis without resection, 6 weeks; minor amputation with a positive bone margin, up to 3 weeks. These are syndrome-specific anchors, not a universal rule. Sources oviva , wiki , nvo , dfi

Evaluate S. aureus bacteremia for an endovascular source. Post-traumatic, postoperative, or hardware-associated infection S. aureus , coagulase-negative staphylococci, gram-negative bacilli; sometimes polymicrobial Use multiple deep operative specimens, not a surface swab. Contiguous diabetic foot osteomyelitis Mild/new: S. aureus and beta-hemolytic streptococci. Chronic, deep, or previously treated: gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes become more likely. Bone culture is preferred when feasible; superficial wound flora can mislead. Pelvic osteomyelitis beneath a pressure injury Often polymicrobial, but exposed bone and wound cultures are heavily colonized Deep bone obtained during planned debridement/closure is the useful specimen. Source Prefer blood cultures when hematogenous disease is plausible and bone or deep operative specimens when available. A superficial swab usually reflects colonizing flora. Duration With adequate source control and no retained implant, treatment generally does not exceed 6 weeks. Complete resection of infected bone may require no osteomyelitis course. Residual soft-tissue infection is treated separately. Route Osteomyelitis does not automatically require a PICC. An active, well-absorbed oral regimen is reasonable when the patient is stable, source control is adequate, absorption is reliable, and adherence and interactions have been addressed. Common anchors: most bacterial vertebral osteomyelitis, 6 weeks; diabetic foot osteomyelitis without resection, 6 weeks; minor amputation with a positive bone margin, up to 3 weeks. These are syndrome-specific anchors, not a universal rule. Sources oviva , wiki , nvo , dfi

slides.title: An open sacral wound without a closure plan is not cured by prolonged antibiotics
slides.section: An open sacral wound without a closure plan is not cured by prolonged antibiotics
rows: Exposed bone or MRI changes, but no acute cellulitis, abscess, bacteremia, or sepsis; debridement and durable closure are not feasible.
Do not give a 6-week osteomyelitis course, repeated courses, or chronic suppression for the wound alone.
Pressure redistribution, wound and moisture care, selective debridement, nutrition, pain and odor control, continence management, and realistic goals of care.

Complete source section:
An open sacral wound without a closure plan is not cured by prolonged antibiotics Three clinically different situations Situation Antibiotics What matters more Exposed bone or MRI changes, but no acute cellulitis, abscess, bacteremia, or sepsis; debridement and durable closure are not feasible. Do not give a 6-week osteomyelitis course, repeated courses, or chronic suppression for the wound alone. slides.title: Case 1 · Crystals in a hot native knee
slides.section: Three cases are enough for the live discussion
paragraphs: A febrile patient has an acutely swollen knee. Synovial fluid contains urate crystals and 72,000 WBC/µL with 92% neutrophils.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Three cases are enough for the live discussion Case 1 · Crystals in a hot native knee A febrile patient has an acutely swollen knee. Synovial fluid contains urate crystals and 72,000 WBC/µL with 92% neutrophils. What should happen next? Crystals do not exclude infection. Send synovial culture and blood cultures, begin empiric therapy after aspiration if stable enough to sample first, and obtain urgent orthopedic input for drainage. Case 2 · Acute postoperative knee PJI Three weeks after TKA, the patient develops 3 days of pain, effusion, and drainage. Components are fixed and aspiration grows MSSA. What determines the plan? This may be a DAIR candidate if there is no sinus tract, soft tissue is suitable, and modular components can be exchanged. Obtain multiple deep cultures. For susceptible staphylococcal knee PJI treated with DAIR, the IDSA rifampin-based regimen completes 6 months. Select an active route and oral transition based on response; rifampin requires an active companion after debridement. Case 3 · Exposed sacral bone without a flap option A chronically immobile patient has an open stage IV sacral wound and MRI changes called osteomyelitis, but no cellulitis, abscess, fever, bacteremia, or instability. Durable closure is not feasible. Would six weeks of antibiotics help? No durable benefit has been shown. Do not treat the imaging label alone. Focus on pressure relief, wound and moisture care, nutrition, debridement when appropriate, symptom control, and goals of care. Treat future discrete cellulitis, abscess, bacteremia, or sepsis episodes when they occur. Closing sentence Name the infected structure, best microbiology, source control completed or impossible, retained material, treatment intent, and the event that determines duration.

slides.title: Classify five things before selecting an antibiotic
slides.section: Classify five things before selecting an antibiotic
paragraphs: What structure? Native joint, prosthesis, bone, spine, diabetic foot, pressure injury, fracture hardware.
What tempo? Hours to days, weeks, or months. Tempo narrows the differential but does not set the treatment clock.
What remains? Pus, necrotic bone, biofilm-coated implant, sinus tract, unstable spine, open wound, ischemic tissue.
Can it be controlled? Drain, debride, exchange, remove, reconstruct, revascularize, or intentionally manage noncuratively.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Classify five things before selecting an antibiotic What structure? Native joint, prosthesis, bone, spine, diabetic foot, pressure injury, fracture hardware. What tempo? Hours to days, weeks, or months. Tempo narrows the differential but does not set the treatment clock. What remains? Pus, necrotic bone, biofilm-coated implant, sinus tract, unstable spine, open wound, ischemic tissue. Can it be controlled? Drain, debride, exchange, remove, reconstruct, revascularize, or intentionally manage noncuratively. What is the intent? Cure, prolonged treatment with retained material, suppression, or treatment of acute flares only. Tempo changes the differential more than it changes the duration Pattern Common examples What it should trigger What it does not prove Acute Hot native joint, acute hematogenous osteomyelitis, early postoperative PJI, acute hematogenous PJI Urgent aspiration/cultures, assessment for bacteremia, prompt drainage or debridement when indicated That a short antibiotic course will be sufficient Subacute Brodie abscess, indolent vertebral infection, delayed PJI Deliberate tissue diagnosis, histology when mimic is possible, surgical planning before empiric therapy if stable That normal WBC/CRP excludes infection Chronic Sinus-tract PJI, sequestrum, chronic post-traumatic osteomyelitis, stage IV pressure injury Identify necrotic bone or retained material and decide whether durable source control is feasible That prolonged antibiotics alone can sterilize an uncorrected source Do not let the MRI choose the treatment MRI is sensitive for osteomyelitis but can remain abnormal during healing and can be difficult to interpret near surgery, hardware, neuropathic bone, or chronic pressure injury. Treat a clinical syndrome with a source-control plan, not an imaging phrase in isolation. Sources wiki , pressure-2019 , pressure-2024

slides.title: Before antibiotics
slides.section: Native septic arthritis is a drainage problem plus an antibiotic problem
paragraphs: Unless the patient is septic or unstable, aspirate the joint promptly before starting antibiotics. Send synovial bacterial culture, cell count with differential, and crystals; obtain blood cultures when febrile, systemically ill, or bacteremia is plausible. A synovial WBC above 50,000/µL increases suspicion but is not diagnostic, a lower count does not exclude infection, and crystals do not exclude concomitant bacterial arthritis.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Native septic arthritis is a drainage problem plus an antibiotic problem Before antibiotics Unless the patient is septic or unstable, aspirate the joint promptly before starting antibiotics. Send synovial bacterial culture, cell count with differential, and crystals; obtain blood cultures when febrile, systemically ill, or bacteremia is plausible. A synovial WBC above 50,000/µL increases suspicion but is not diagnostic, a lower count does not exclude infection, and crystals do not exclude concomitant bacterial arthritis. Gram stain has limited sensitivity but useful specificity. If the joint is difficult to access, image-guided aspiration is reasonable. Sacroiliac, sternoclavicular, and other axial infections deserve early assessment for adjacent osteomyelitis, abscess, or endovascular source. Practical adult native-joint treatment framework Situation Initial approach Source control Typical duration framework Unstable, sepsis, or septic shock Obtain blood cultures and aspirate if this will not meaningfully delay therapy. A common US empiric regimen is vancomycin plus ceftriaxone; use cefepime or another antipseudomonal beta-lactam when resistant gram-negative/Pseudomonas risk is substantial. Urgent orthopedic evaluation and lavage/drainage. Define after organism, drainage, bacteremia, and adjacent infection are known. Stable, no resistant gram-negative risk Aspirate first. Empiric vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is reasonable pending Gram stain and cultures, then narrow promptly. Arthroscopic lavage is commonly preferred for large joints; open debridement may be needed for advanced disease, adhesions, or bone/cartilage destruction. SANJO suggests 1–2 weeks IV followed by 2–4 weeks oral when improving. Evidence is low. Shorter total courses are best supported for hand/wrist infection after adequate drainage. MSSA Cefazolin or an antistaphylococcal penicillin. Drainage remains essential. Usually measured in weeks, not days. Extend for bacteremia complications, adjacent osteomyelitis, delayed drainage, or poor response. MRSA Vancomycin or daptomycin when appropriate; tailor to susceptibility, renal function, bacteremia, and local practice. Drainage remains essential. Often 3–4 weeks for uncomplicated drained arthritis, longer when complicated. Evidence is limited. Streptococci Penicillin/ampicillin or ceftriaxone when susceptible. Drainage. Usually several weeks; clinical response and complexity matter. Enteric gram-negative bacilli Ceftriaxone, cefepime, a carbapenem, or other active beta-lactam according to resistance pattern and syndrome. Active fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX can be oral completion options in selected patients. Drainage; investigate urinary, abdominal, or bloodstream source when appropriate. Often 3–4 weeks when uncomplicated and well drained; longer for associated endovascular infection, adjacent osteomyelitis, inadequate source control, or a poor clinical response. Pseudomonas Active cefepime, ceftazidime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or another susceptibility-guided antipseudomonal agent; ciprofloxacin can be a high-bioavailability oral option if susceptible and clinically appropriate. Drainage. Commonly 4–6 weeks when complicated. Do not extend merely because the organism is Pseudomonas if the clinical course is uncomplicated and source control is excellent. Gonococcal arthritis / arthritis-dermatitis Ceftriaxone 1 g IV or IM every 24 hours. Treat chlamydia with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days if not excluded. Purulent joints may require serial aspiration or operative drainage. After substantial improvement, susceptibility-guided oral transition can occur at 24–48 hours; total treatment is at least 7 days. The two-week trial is easy to overgeneralize A randomized trial found 2 weeks noninferior to 4 weeks after surgical drainage, but 99 of 154 cases involved the hand or wrist. It should not be used as blanket evidence for two weeks in a bacteremic native knee, shoulder, hip, axial joint, or infection with adjacent osteomyelitis. Failure to improve should trigger repeat examination and reassessment of drainage, not automatic broadening or extension. Sources sanjo , 2v4 , gono

slides.title: The operation determines the antibiotic strategy in PJI
slides.section: The operation determines the antibiotic strategy in PJI
rows: Acute symptoms for less than about 3 weeks or early postoperative PJI within about 4 weeks; fixed implant, no sinus, acceptable soft tissue, and a usable biofilm-active oral regimen.

Open debridement with polyethylene/modular exchange when feasible. Use pathogen-directed therapy; an active oral transition depends on the organism, patient, surgical response, and regimen. For susceptible staphylococci, use rifampin only with an active companion after debridement.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
The operation determines the antibiotic strategy in PJI Operative pathways and antibiotic timing Strategy Best fit Immediate postoperative phase Total course and reimplantation plan DAIR with modular-component exchange Acute symptoms for less than about 3 weeks or early postoperative PJI within about 4 weeks; fixed implant, no sinus, acceptable soft tissue, and a usable biofilm-active oral regimen. Open debridement with polyethylene/modular exchange when feasible. Use pathogen-directed therapy; an active oral transition depends on the organism, patient, surgical response, and regimen. For susceptible staphylococci, use rifampin only with an active companion after debridement. The IDSA staphylococcal rifampin-based regimen completes 3 months for hip or 6 months for knee . Other regimens need separate duration decisions. A defined curative course is not indefinite suppression. One-stage exchange Selected chronic PJI with good soft tissue, no sinus tract or major reconstructive barrier, and a known, susceptible, readily treatable organism. Remove all infected components, perform radical debridement, obtain at least 5 deep specimens with separate instruments, and implant the new prosthesis in the same operation. Use organism-directed therapy. Transition to an active oral agent may be appropriate, but no fixed IV lead-in applies to all cases. IDSA describes 2–6 weeks of IV therapy with rifampin, followed by an oral companion and rifampin to complete 3 months for susceptible staphylococci, and 4–6 weeks of pathogen-directed therapy for other organisms. Longer courses require case-specific justification; indefinite suppression is a separate decision. Two-stage exchange: first stage Chronic PJI, compromised soft tissue, difficult or unknown organism, major bone loss, or failed DAIR/one-stage strategy. Remove prosthesis, debride, obtain deep specimens, and place an antibiotic spacer when appropriate. Give pathogen-directed therapy; IDSA permits IV or highly bioavailable oral treatment. Route and transition depend on the organism, patient, and regimen. IDSA recommends 4–6 weeks after resection. The need and length of any antibiotic-free period before reimplantation are uncertain; no fixed holiday is established. Two-stage exchange: reimplantation Clinical course, soft tissue, surgical findings, inflammatory markers, and any aspiration/culture data support infection control. Obtain multiple deep specimens at reimplantation. Give indicated perioperative surgical prophylaxis when the prior infection is believed eradicated. This is distinct from restarting a prolonged therapeutic course; base that decision on operative findings, microbiology, and the joint-team assessment. Concordant growth in at least 2 specimens supports persistent infection. Do not dismiss a single virulent isolate such as S. aureus ; interpret it with histology, operative findings, and the joint-team assessment. Decide the need and duration of additional treatment case by case. Negative cultures without residual infection do not by themselves justify prolonged postoperative therapy. Resection arthroplasty / arthrodesis / amputation When reconstruction is not feasible, repeated curative attempts have failed, or patient goals favor definitive source removal. Obtain deep cultures and treat residual infection. The initial IV-to-oral decision follows stability, source control, susceptibility, absorption, and drug interactions. Usually 4–6 weeks if residual infected tissue remains. If all infected tissue is removed and there is no bacteremia or residual soft-tissue infection, prolonged therapy may not be needed. No curative surgery Operative risk, patient preference, or anatomy makes curative source control unacceptable. Treat acute sepsis, abscess, or bacteremia first and obtain the best possible microbiology. Then consider culture-directed suppressive therapy only if there is a defined organism, active tolerable oral option, and meaningful functional goal. Suppression is noncurative and can fail from resistance, toxicity, loosening, sinus formation, or progression. Local standard for DAIR For susceptible staphylococcal DAIR treated with a rifampin-based regimen, IDSA recommends 3 months for hip and 6 months for knee. DATIPO did not establish noninferiority of 6 versus 12 weeks across surgically managed PJI. Duration for other organisms and regimens needs case-specific review. Do not overgeneralize SOLARIO SOLARIO found that no more than 7 days of systemic antibiotics was noninferior to at least 4 weeks after definitive curative surgery plus a local antibiotic carrier. DAIR and suppressive procedures were excluded, and the PJI subgroup was small and not independently powered. The trial is practice-informing for carefully selected definitive surgery, but it does not shorten the local DAIR, one-stage, or two-stage pathways. Rifampin rules Use rifampin for a susceptible staphylococcal biofilm infection only as part of combination therapy. Never use rifampin monotherapy. Do not add it empirically before knowing the organism. Reduce the bacterial burden surgically first. Review drug interactions, hepatotoxicity, absorption, and companion-drug activity. Fluoroquinolones have the strongest companion evidence, but other agents are used when appropriate. The exact best time to start rifampin is not established. A rigid postoperative day rule is not evidence based. Sources pji-2013 , datipo , solario , wiki , pji-review

slides.title: Local standard for DAIR
slides.section: The operation determines the antibiotic strategy in PJI
paragraphs: For susceptible staphylococcal DAIR treated with a rifampin-based regimen, IDSA recommends 3 months for hip and 6 months for knee. DATIPO did not establish noninferiority of 6 versus 12 weeks across surgically managed PJI. Duration for other organisms and regimens needs case-specific review.

Complete source section:
The operation determines the antibiotic strategy in PJI Operative pathways and antibiotic timing Strategy Best fit Immediate postoperative phase Total course and reimplantation plan DAIR with modular-component exchange Acute symptoms for less than about 3 weeks or early postoperative PJI within about 4 weeks; fixed implant, no sinus, acceptable soft tissue, and a usable biofilm-active oral regimen. Open debridement with polyethylene/modular exchange when feasible. Use pathogen-directed therapy; an active oral transition depends on the organism, patient, surgical response, and regimen. For susceptible staphylococci, use rifampin only with an active companion after debridement. The IDSA staphylococcal rifampin-based regimen completes 3 months for hip or 6 months for knee . Other regimens need separate duration decisions. A defined curative course is not indefinite suppression. One-stage exchange Selected chronic PJI with good soft tissue, no sinus tract or major reconstructive barrier, and a known, susceptible, readily treatable organism. Remove all infected components, perform radical debridement, obtain at least 5 deep specimens with separate instruments, and implant the new prosthesis in the same operation. Use organism-directed therapy. Transition to an active oral agent may be appropriate, but no fixed IV lead-in applies to all cases. IDSA describes 2–6 weeks of IV therapy with rifampin, followed by an oral companion and rifampin to complete 3 months for susceptible staphylococci, and 4–6 weeks of pathogen-directed therapy for other organisms. Longer courses require case-specific justification; indefinite suppression is a separate decision. Two-stage exchange: first stage Chronic PJI, compromised soft tissue, difficult or unknown organism, major bone loss, or failed DAIR/one-stage strategy. Remove prosthesis, debride, obtain deep specimens, and place an antibiotic spacer when appropriate. Give pathogen-directed therapy; IDSA permits IV or highly bioavailable oral treatment. Route and transition depend on the organism, patient, and regimen. IDSA recommends 4–6 weeks after resection. The need and length of any antibiotic-free period before reimplantation are uncertain; no fixed holiday is established. Obtain multiple deep specimens at reimplantation. Give indicated perioperative surgical prophylaxis when the prior infection is believed eradicated. This is distinct from restarting a prolonged therapeutic course; base that decision on operative findings, microbiology, and the joint-team assessment. Concordant growth in at least 2 specimens supports persistent infection. Usually 4–6 weeks if residual infected tissue remains. If all infected tissue is removed and there is no bacteremia or residual soft-tissue infection, prolonged therapy may not be needed. Then consider culture-directed suppressive therapy only if there is a defined organism, active tolerable oral option, and meaningful functional goal. DAIR and suppressive procedures were excluded, and the PJI subgroup was small and not independently powered. slides.title: Osteomyelitis without a retained implant usually does not need more than six weeks
slides.section: Osteomyelitis without a retained implant usually does not need more than six weeks
paragraphs: First define the route and anatomy: hematogenous, contiguous/post-traumatic, diabetic foot, vertebral, pressure-injury pelvic osteomyelitis, or hardware-associated infection. Chronic osteomyelitis with a sequestrum behaves differently from acute hematogenous disease even if the same organism is isolated.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Osteomyelitis without a retained implant usually does not need more than six weeks First define the route and anatomy: hematogenous, contiguous/post-traumatic, diabetic foot, vertebral, pressure-injury pelvic osteomyelitis, or hardware-associated infection. Chronic osteomyelitis with a sequestrum behaves differently from acute hematogenous disease even if the same organism is isolated. Management by source-control state Scenario Diagnostic priority Non-ID treatment Antibiotic duration framework Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis Blood cultures; MRI when needed; tissue diagnosis if blood cultures do not establish the pathogen and biopsy will change management. Drain abscess; debride necrotic tissue when present. Evaluate endovascular source for S. aureus bacteremia. Generally up to 6 weeks when no retained implant and source control is adequate. Oral therapy can be used when criteria are met. Subacute osteomyelitis / Brodie abscess Imaging plus biopsy/curettage when feasible because tumor and other mimics can resemble infection. Systemic inflammatory signs are often absent. Curettage/debridement is common, both diagnostic and therapeutic. No high-quality duration standard. Culture-directed therapy is commonly 4–6 weeks after curettage, but published practice is heterogeneous. Chronic contiguous or post-traumatic osteomyelitis with sequestrum Deep bone/tissue culture and histology at debridement. Surface swabs are weak etiologic specimens. Remove necrotic bone, drain abscess, manage dead space, remove infected hardware when feasible, stabilize bone, and obtain durable vascularized soft-tissue coverage. Usually no more than 6 weeks after adequate source control. Three to four weeks may be adequate after debridement in selected cases, but confirmatory evidence is limited. Complete resection of infected bone Confirm that residual infected bone and soft-tissue infection are absent. Definitive resection/amputation plus wound management. General pyogenic osteomyelitis guidance permits no further osteomyelitis treatment after complete resection when no soft-tissue infection remains. For diabetes-related foot osteomyelitis, the IWGDF/IDSA table specifies 2–5 days after complete resection; positive margins and residual soft-tissue infection require their own courses. Retained fracture fixation hardware Deep cultures, union status, stability, and whether hardware can be removed without mechanical failure. Debridement and stabilization. Sometimes hardware must remain until union, then can be removed. Evidence is weaker. Therapy may need to continue through fracture healing and/or transition to suppression until hardware can safely be removed. Coordinate with orthopedics rather than applying a PJI algorithm automatically. Diabetic foot osteomyelitis deserves its own pathway The current 2023 IWGDF/IDSA guideline recommends probe-to-bone, plain radiographs, and ESR/CRP/PCT as initial studies, followed by MRI when doubt persists. Obtain bone rather than soft-tissue culture when feasible. For mild infection in North America, initially target aerobic gram-positive pathogens; do not empirically cover Pseudomonas in a temperate climate unless recent cultures or a specific exposure supports it. For osteomyelitis treated without bone resection or amputation, use 6 weeks. After minor amputation with a positive bone-margin culture, use up to 3 weeks. Antibiotic-only treatment is most defensible for selected forefoot osteomyelitis without an urgent drainage need, peripheral arterial disease, or exposed bone. slides.title: Stable vertebral osteomyelitis is one of the situations where delaying empiric therapy can improve the diagnosis
slides.section: Stable vertebral osteomyelitis is one of the situations where delaying empiric therapy can improve the diagnosis
paragraphs: Obtain blood cultures and MRI. S. aureus bacteremia with a compatible MRI often establishes the diagnosis without disc-space biopsy. If the patient is hemodynamically stable with a stable neurologic examination and blood cultures are nondiagnostic, the IDSA guideline supports withholding empiric therapy while obtaining a microbiologic diagnosis. Sepsis, shock, or severe/progressive neurologic symptoms require prompt treatment while the diagnostic workup proceeds.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Stable vertebral osteomyelitis is one of the situations where delaying empiric therapy can improve the diagnosis Obtain blood cultures and MRI. S. aureus bacteremia with a compatible MRI often establishes the diagnosis without disc-space biopsy. If the patient is hemodynamically stable with a stable neurologic examination and blood cultures are nondiagnostic, the IDSA guideline supports withholding empiric therapy while obtaining a microbiologic diagnosis. Sepsis, shock, or severe/progressive neurologic symptoms require prompt treatment while the diagnostic workup proceeds. Medical treatment For most bacterial native vertebral osteomyelitis, use 6 weeks of parenteral or highly bioavailable oral therapy. Routine extension beyond 6 weeks because MRI still looks abnormal is not supported. Call spine surgery early for Progressive neurologic deficit, progressive deformity, spinal instability, persistent/recurrent bacteremia without another source, or worsening pain despite appropriate therapy. Follow the patient clinically. ESR/CRP can support trend assessment, but persistent pain, an elevated marker, or residual MRI abnormalities alone do not establish treatment failure. Source nvo

slides.title: Medical treatment
slides.section: Stable vertebral osteomyelitis is one of the situations where delaying empiric therapy can improve the diagnosis
paragraphs: For most bacterial native vertebral osteomyelitis, use 6 weeks of parenteral or highly bioavailable oral therapy. Routine extension beyond 6 weeks because MRI still looks abnormal is not supported.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Stable vertebral osteomyelitis is one of the situations where delaying empiric therapy can improve the diagnosis Obtain blood cultures and MRI. S. aureus bacteremia with a compatible MRI often establishes the diagnosis without disc-space biopsy. If the patient is hemodynamically stable with a stable neurologic examination and blood cultures are nondiagnostic, the IDSA guideline supports withholding empiric therapy while obtaining a microbiologic diagnosis. Sepsis, shock, or severe/progressive neurologic symptoms require prompt treatment while the diagnostic workup proceeds. Medical treatment For most bacterial native vertebral osteomyelitis, use 6 weeks of parenteral or highly bioavailable oral therapy. Routine extension beyond 6 weeks because MRI still looks abnormal is not supported. Call spine surgery early for Progressive neurologic deficit, progressive deformity, spinal instability, persistent/recurrent bacteremia without another source, or worsening pain despite appropriate therapy. Follow the patient clinically. ESR/CRP can support trend assessment, but persistent pain, an elevated marker, or residual MRI abnormalities alone do not establish treatment failure. Source nvo

slides.title: Chronic sacral or pelvic osteomyelitis with an open pressure wound is not a six-week-antibiotic diagnosis
slides.section: Chronic sacral or pelvic osteomyelitis with an open pressure wound is not a six-week-antibiotic diagnosis
paragraphs: Exposed bone does not prove osteomyelitis. Chronically exposed bone can show reactive remodeling, and MRI may not reliably distinguish that from infection. If the wound cannot be debrided and durably closed, evidence has not shown that prolonged antibiotics sterilize the underlying bone or improve durable outcomes. The treatment goal becomes wound stability, symptom control, prevention of new pressure injury, and treatment of discrete acute infections.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Chronic sacral or pelvic osteomyelitis with an open pressure wound is not a six-week-antibiotic diagnosis Exposed bone does not prove osteomyelitis. Chronically exposed bone can show reactive remodeling, and MRI may not reliably distinguish that from infection. If the wound cannot be debrided and durably closed, evidence has not shown that prolonged antibiotics sterilize the underlying bone or improve durable outcomes. The treatment goal becomes wound stability, symptom control, prevention of new pressure injury, and treatment of discrete acute infections. Stage IV sacral/pelvic pressure injury: when antibiotics help and when they do not Clinical scenario Systemic antibiotics What matters more Exposed bone, chronic wound, no cellulitis, abscess, bacteremia, or systemic illness; no plan for debridement/flap closure None. Do not treat the exposed bone or MRI result with a chronic osteomyelitis course. Pressure redistribution, wound cleansing/dressings and exudate control, debridement of devitalized tissue when appropriate, moisture/incontinence management, nutrition, pain/odor control, rehabilitation and caregiver feasibility, and goals of care. Pelvic osteomyelitis suspected or diagnosed, but no soft-tissue infection and no plan for debridement plus flap reconstruction None. Current evidence does not support prolonged systemic antibiotics. Reassess whether closure is feasible with plastics/wound surgery. If not, manage the chronic wound rather than trying to sterilize an open contaminated surface. Acute cellulitis/soft-tissue infection extending from the ulcer, no abscess About 5 days is a reasonable standard if improving; extend for slow clinical response. Choose coverage from severity, prior cultures, healthcare exposure, and local ecology. Debride necrotic tissue if needed, optimize wound care, pressure relief, and evaluate for deeper collection. Drainable abscess Drain first. About 5–10 days after drainage for the soft-tissue component is typical, individualized to response. Drainage is the key intervention. Obtain a meaningful deep specimen. Pyomyositis Usually 14–21 days, with drainage when an abscess is present. Drainage and assessment for bacteremia/endovascular source. Sepsis or bacteremia plausibly arising from an infected pressure injury Start prompt broad empiric therapy after blood/deep cultures when feasible. A common severe-infection approach is vancomycin plus cefepime plus metronidazole, or vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam, modified for prior resistant isolates and local antibiogram. Narrow quickly. Look for abscess, necrotizing infection, fecal/urinary contamination, or another source. Treat the systemic syndrome and source. Do not automatically convert clinical improvement into six weeks of therapy. Debridement and flap reconstruction planned When stable, hold unnecessary empiric antibiotics until operative deep bone/tissue cultures if feasible. After adequate debridement and flap coverage, 6 weeks remains a conventional standard. Selected cortical-only disease may need less, but evidence for 2–4 weeks is not yet strong enough to use as a universal default. Multidisciplinary surgery, durable coverage, pressure offloading, nutritional optimization, continence management, and a realistic postoperative pressure-relief plan. Do not substitute suppressive antibiotics for wound closure Long-term suppression is sometimes rational for a retained infected orthopedic implant or extensive necrotic bone that cannot be removed. That logic should not be automatically transferred to an open stage IV sacral wound. Ongoing contamination and absent coverage make durable microbial suppression unlikely, and the best available reviews recommend no systemic antibiotics in the absence of an acute soft-tissue/systemic infection or a reconstructive surgical plan. Non-ID treatment is the treatment Pressure and wound mechanics Regular pressure redistribution/repositioning, appropriate support surface, minimizing shear, absorbent dressings, moisture balance, and reducing dressing trauma/frequency when palliation is the goal. Debridement and reconstruction Wound surgery/plastics evaluation for debridement, bone resection when needed, and flap coverage. Assess whether postoperative offloading and wound protection are realistically sustainable before major reconstruction. Host optimization Nutrition and protein/calorie adequacy, perfusion, smoking cessation when relevant, glycemic management, management of spasticity/contractures, urinary/fecal incontinence, pain, odor, mobility, and caregiver resources. Sources pressure-2019 , pressure-2024

slides.title: Choose the antibiotic from the pathogen, site, retained material, and route plan
slides.section: Choose the antibiotic from the pathogen, site, retained material, and route plan
paragraphs: The table below is a treatment framework, not a substitute for susceptibility testing or syndrome-specific dosing. Deep specimens are particularly important in chronic infection.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Choose the antibiotic from the pathogen, site, retained material, and route plan The table below is a treatment framework, not a substitute for susceptibility testing or syndrome-specific dosing. Deep specimens are particularly important in chronic infection. Pathogen clues and common definitive choices Pathogen Common definitive options Oral strategy when appropriate Special issue MSSA Acute native joint, acute hematogenous osteomyelitis, early or hematogenous PJI Cefazolin, nafcillin, or oxacillin. Selected patients can complete with a clinically validated active oral regimen. For retained staphylococcal prostheses, rifampin-combination strategy is a separate biofilm decision. A positive blood culture changes the workup. MRSA Same syndromes as MSSA; risk rises with prior colonization/infection and healthcare exposure Vancomycin or daptomycin; other agents depend on syndrome and susceptibility. Linezolid, TMP-SMX, or doxycycline/minocycline can be used in selected bone/joint regimens when active and clinically appropriate. Check bacteremia/endocarditis, drug toxicity, MIC context, and retained hardware. Coagulase-negative staphylococci Indolent postoperative infection and chronic PJI Vancomycin initially when methicillin resistance is possible; use cefazolin or an antistaphylococcal penicillin if susceptible. Doxycycline/minocycline, TMP-SMX, linezolid, or a beta-lactam when susceptible and clinically appropriate. Repeated concordant deep cultures help distinguish pathogen from contamination. Consider rifampin combination therapy when susceptible staphylococcal hardware is retained. Cutibacterium acnes Especially indolent shoulder PJI Penicillin G or ceftriaxone are common IV choices. Amoxicillin, cefadroxil, clindamycin, or doxycycline according to susceptibility and tolerance. Request prolonged anaerobic incubation and interpret multiple specimens in the surgical context. Streptococci Native-joint infection and acute hematogenous PJI, sometimes from skin or oral source Penicillin/ampicillin or ceftriaxone; cefazolin for susceptible isolates is also reasonable. Amoxicillin can be useful for susceptible organisms when oral therapy is appropriate. Implant infection still depends heavily on operative strategy. Enterococcus PJI or contiguous infection with urinary, gastrointestinal, or healthcare association Ampicillin when susceptible; vancomycin when needed. Linezolid or high-dose daptomycin are common VRE options. Linezolid has high bioavailability; amoxicillin can be used for susceptible isolates in selected settings. Endovascular infection may require a different regimen. Enterobacterales Older or immunocompromised host, urinary/intra-abdominal bacteremia, DFO, or postoperative infection Ceftriaxone, cefepime, carbapenem, or other active beta-lactam according to resistance mechanism and site. Fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX when susceptible, tolerated, and appropriate. ESBL, AmpC, or CRE may change the preferred beta-lactam. Pseudomonas aeruginosa Healthcare exposure, penetrating injury, selected injection-drug or water exposures; not routine empiric DFO coverage in Missouri Cefepime, ceftazidime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or a newer active agent depending on resistance. slides.title: Suppression is a treatment intent, not a longer version of curative therapy
slides.section: Suppression is a treatment intent, not a longer version of curative therapy
paragraphs: Suppressive antimicrobial therapy is reasonable to consider when infected hardware or necrotic bone cannot be removed, curative surgery is too risky or declined, the organism is known, and a tolerable active oral agent exists. The goal is to reduce relapse, symptoms, or additional surgery. It does not sterilize the retained source.

paragraphs: In 1,054 adults with complex orthopedic infection, definitive treatment failure occurred in 14.6% assigned to IV therapy and 13.2% assigned to oral therapy during the first 6 weeks. Oral therapy met noninferiority criteria. Catheter complications were more common with IV treatment, 9.4% versus 1.0%. This supports carefully selected oral regimens. It does not mean every oral drug is adequate or that source control can be omitted.

Complete source section:

It does not mean every oral drug is adequate or that source control can be omitted. DATIPO: six weeks was not enough for all surgically managed PJI The randomized PJI trial failed to show noninferiority of 6 weeks compared with 12 weeks. The signal was most concerning with retained-implant strategies such as DAIR. It supports avoiding a 6-week DAIR course, but it does not establish one universal duration for every joint or exchange strategy. The 2013 IDSA staphylococcal rifampin-based regimen specifies 3 months for hip and 6 months for knee DAIR. SOLARIO: very short systemic therapy after definitive surgery plus local antibiotics In 475 eligible adults who underwent definitive curative surgery, received a local antibiotic carrier eluting for at least 4 weeks, and achieved primary closure, no more than 7 days of systemic therapy was noninferior to at least 4 weeks for definite failure at 12 months (11.1% versus 14.1%). slides.title: Case 1 · Crystals and a hot knee
slides.section: Cases: decide the source-control plan before the antibiotic clock
paragraphs: A 67-year-old has fever and an acutely swollen native knee. Synovial fluid contains urate crystals and 72,000 WBC/µL with 92% neutrophils.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Cases: decide the source-control plan before the antibiotic clock Case 1 · Crystals and a hot knee A 67-year-old has fever and an acutely swollen native knee. Synovial fluid contains urate crystals and 72,000 WBC/µL with 92% neutrophils. Discuss the decision Crystals do not exclude septic arthritis. Send Gram stain/culture and blood cultures, start empiric therapy after aspiration if stable enough to sample first, and obtain urgent orthopedic input for drainage. Narrow to the organism. Case 2 · Arthritis plus pustules A young adult has migratory arthralgia, tenosynovitis, pustular lesions, and a swollen ankle. Discuss the decision Evaluate for disseminated gonococcal infection. Obtain NAAT from exposed mucosal sites, culture of purulent material when possible, and blood cultures when appropriate. Treat with ceftriaxone 1 g every 24 hours; treat chlamydia if not excluded. Total therapy is at least 7 days, with susceptibility-guided oral transition after substantial improvement. Case 3 · Acute postoperative knee PJI Three weeks after TKA, the patient develops 3 days of pain, effusion, and drainage. Components are well fixed. Aspiration grows MSSA. Discuss the decision This is a favorable timing pattern for DAIR if the soft tissue and implant are otherwise suitable. Exchange modular components when feasible, obtain multiple deep cultures, and use pathogen-directed therapy. For susceptible staphylococcal knee PJI treated with DAIR, the IDSA rifampin-based regimen completes 6 months. The route and timing of oral transition depend on clinical response and an active companion drug. Add rifampin only as combination therapy after debridement. Case 4 · Chronic hip PJI considered for one-stage exchange A patient has months of hip pain, a well-fixed prosthesis, good soft tissue, no sinus tract, and repeated deep aspiration cultures growing susceptible Cutibacterium acnes . Discuss the decision This is a potential one-stage exchange candidate because the organism is known and tractable and the soft-tissue envelope is favorable. Remove all infected components, perform radical debridement, obtain at least 5 deep specimens with separate instruments, and implant the new prosthesis during the same operation. Choose a pathogen-directed regimen and duration after reviewing operative cultures. For this nonstaphylococcal example, IDSA describes 4–6 weeks of IV or highly bioavailable oral therapy; a fixed IV lead-in is not established. Indefinite suppression is a separate decision. Case 5 · Stable vertebral osteomyelitis with negative blood cultures A stable patient has severe back pain and MRI findings compatible with L2–L3 discitis/osteomyelitis. Neurologic examination is normal and blood cultures are negative. Discuss the decision If clinically safe, do not rush into empiric six-week therapy before obtaining a microbiologic diagnosis. Arrange image-guided biopsy and assess alternative diagnoses. If bacterial NVO is confirmed, most patients need 6 weeks of parenteral or highly bioavailable oral therapy. Repeat MRI is not routine if the patient improves. slides.title: Check the reasoning
slides.section: Check the reasoning
paragraphs: 1. Do urate crystals exclude septic arthritis?
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Check the reasoning 1. Do urate crystals exclude septic arthritis? Show explanation No. Crystal disease and bacterial arthritis can coexist. 2. What is the highest-value action in a purulent native knee? Show explanation Prompt diagnostic sampling and effective drainage, with timely active antibiotics. Antibiotics do not substitute for drainage. 3. Does every acute PJI qualify for DAIR? Show explanation No. Implant stability, symptom duration, sinus tract, soft tissue, pathogen, host factors, and ability to exchange modular parts all affect the likelihood of cure. 4. Is rifampin a general add-on for any staphylococcal bone infection? Show explanation No. Its strongest clinical role is susceptible staphylococcal infection with retained prosthetic material in combination with another active agent. Never use it alone. 5. Does osteomyelitis require six weeks of IV therapy? Show explanation No. Six weeks is a common maximum for adequately source-controlled osteomyelitis without retained implant, and validated oral regimens are reasonable in selected patients. Complete resection may need no osteomyelitis therapy at all. 6. Does exposed sacral bone prove osteomyelitis? Show explanation No. Chronic exposed bone can show remodeling without histologic osteomyelitis, and MRI can overcall infection in this setting. 7. What should an asymptomatic open sacral wound with suspected pelvic osteomyelitis receive if there is no debridement/flap plan? Show explanation No systemic antibiotics for the osteomyelitis label alone. Treat acute soft-tissue or systemic infections when present and focus on wound/pressure management. 8. When is chronic suppression most defensible? Show explanation When a defined infection source such as retained prosthetic hardware cannot be removed, a known pathogen has a tolerable active oral option, and preventing relapse or further surgery is a meaningful patient goal. 9. Should worsening vertebral MRI at week 6 automatically extend antibiotics? Show explanation No. If pain, examination, and inflammatory markers are improving, imaging can lag behind clinical cure. 10. What is the central documentation sentence? Show explanation State the infected structure, source control completed or impossible, microbiologic target, treatment intent, and what event determines duration.

Show explanation No. Chronic exposed bone can show remodeling without histologic osteomyelitis, and MRI can overcall infection in this setting. 7. What should an asymptomatic open sacral wound with suspected pelvic osteomyelitis receive if there is no debridement/flap plan? Show explanation No systemic antibiotics for the osteomyelitis label alone. Treat acute soft-tissue or systemic infections when present and focus on wound/pressure management. 8. When is chronic suppression most defensible? Show explanation When a defined infection source such as retained prosthetic hardware cannot be removed, a known pathogen has a tolerable active oral option, and preventing relapse or further surgery is a meaningful patient goal. 9. Should worsening vertebral MRI at week 6 automatically extend antibiotics? Show explanation No. If pain, examination, and inflammatory markers are improving, imaging can lag behind clinical cure. 10. slides.title: Bone and joint infections · One-page rounds sheet
slides.section: Bone and joint infections · One-page rounds sheet
paragraphs: September 21, 2026 · Teaching companion. Specialty review pending.

Aspirate before antibiotics if stable. Send culture, WBC/diff, crystals. Crystals do not exclude infection. Drain the joint. Empiric vancomycin + ceftriaxone is a common US starting point; use antipseudomonal coverage when risk warrants.

Sinus tract to prosthesis = PJI. If stable, avoid premature antibiotics. Aspirate when useful. At surgery obtain multiple deep samples, ideally 5–6. Do not use superficial sinus/wound swab to choose long-term therapy.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Bone and joint infections · One-page rounds sheet September 21, 2026 · Teaching companion. Specialty review pending. Native septic arthritis Aspirate before antibiotics if stable. Send culture, WBC/diff, crystals. Crystals do not exclude infection. Drain the joint. Empiric vancomycin + ceftriaxone is a common US starting point; use antipseudomonal coverage when risk warrants. PJI diagnosis Sinus tract to prosthesis = PJI. If stable, avoid premature antibiotics. Aspirate when useful. At surgery obtain multiple deep samples, ideally 5–6. Do not use superficial sinus/wound swab to choose long-term therapy. PJI surgery DAIR: acute, brief symptoms, fixed implant, no sinus, good tissue, exchange modular parts. One-stage: selected chronic PJI with known/tractable organism and good tissue. Two-stage: chronic/difficult infection, compromised tissue, or failed retention. PJI antibiotics Staphylococcal DAIR: IDSA rifampin-based regimen totals 3 months for hip or 6 months for knee. One-stage duration differs by pathogen and regimen. Two-stage after explant: IDSA recommends 4–6 weeks of pathogen-directed IV or highly bioavailable oral therapy; a fixed antibiotic holiday is not established. Positive reimplantation cultures need case-specific assessment. Give indicated perioperative prophylaxis. Osteomyelitis, no implant Culture meaningful tissue, drain abscess, remove necrotic bone. With adequate source control, generally ≤6 weeks. After complete resection without residual infection, diabetes-related foot guidance lists 2–5 days; general pyogenic osteomyelitis guidance permits no further course in selected cases. Vertebral osteomyelitis Stable neuro/hemodynamics: obtain microbiologic diagnosis before empiric therapy when possible. Most bacterial NVO = 6 weeks IV or highly bioavailable oral. Diabetic foot DFO without resection = 6 weeks. Minor amputation + positive bone margin = up to 3 weeks. Pair antibiotics with debridement, offloading, wound care, and vascular assessment when ischemic. Stage IV sacral/pelvic wound Exposed bone or MRI “OM” without acute infection and without debridement/flap plan = no systemic antibiotics. Treat discrete cellulitis, abscess, bacteremia, or sepsis. If debridement + flap occurs, ~6 weeks remains conventional. Oral therapy OVIVA supports oral treatment when stable, source controlled, absorbing reliably, and an active evidence-supported oral drug is available. Osteomyelitis does not automatically require a PICC. Suppression Noncurative. Best fit: defined pathogen + retained hardware/necrotic source that cannot be removed + tolerable active oral drug + meaningful goal. Do not routinely suppress an open sacral pressure wound.
